meaning: “Not to mention A, even B …”, or “it goes without saying” / “better left unsaid”. Written and rather elegant.
connection: Noun + は言わずもがな, noun + も／まで; 言わずもがなのこと

senses.label: Not to mention A
senses.meaning: The first item is obvious, and the second goes further. Like “not to mention A, even B …”. The second part usually takes 「も」 or 「まで」. More elegant than 「〜は言うまでもなく」.
senses.connection: Noun + は言わずもがな, noun + も／まで
examples: The food here goes without saying, and the service is first-rate too.
She speaks English, of course, and French and Chinese as well.
It's a game that hooks adults, let alone kids.

senses.label: It goes without saying
senses.meaning: “Everyone knows this without being told.” Often used as an opener: 「言わずもがなだ」, 「言わずもがなのことだが」. Formal; used to remind people of something well known.
senses.connection: 〜のは言わずもがなだ; 言わずもがなのことだが、〜
examples: It goes without saying that health matters more than anything.
This should go without saying, but please be sure to meet the deadline.

senses.label: Better left unsaid
senses.meaning: The original meaning: “better not said, no need to say it”. Usually 「言わずもがなのことを言う」, saying something you should have kept to yourself. Carries regret or criticism.
senses.connection: 言わずもがなのこと + を言う／を口にする
examples: I let slip something better left unsaid and made him angry.
At the meeting he added one remark that was better left unsaid.

notes: What 「言わずもがなのこと」 means depends on the verb that follows. 「言わずもがなのことですが」 is an opener meaning “this should go without saying”; 「言わずもがなのことを言ってしまった」 means “I said something I should have kept to myself,” with self-reproach or criticism. The two point in opposite directions, so don't mix them up.
Telling a superior or client 「それは言わずもがなでしょう」 amounts to “well, obviously,” which sounds condescending and rude. To remind someone of something, 「念のため申し上げますが」 is safer.
A must be the more obvious item, and the second part needs 「も」 or 「まで」 to echo it: ✕「味は言わずもがな、サービスは一流だ」→ ○「味は言わずもがな、サービスも一流だ」.
When the second part is negative or means “can't even …,” 「はおろか」 is the usual choice: 「漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない」 sounds more natural than using 「言わずもがな」.

daily.title: Recommending a restaurant
daily.description: Telling a friend about a favorite place.
daily.example: The food there goes without saying, and the atmosphere is great too.

daily.title: Regretting your words
daily.description: After a fight with a friend, telling family you said too much.
daily.example: I even said things better left unsaid, and I regret it.

daily.title: Seen in reviews
daily.description: Book or film reviews praising a work.
daily.example: The lead's acting goes without saying, and the supporting cast also stands out.

work.title: Reminder at a meeting
work.description: The chair reminds attendees of a well-known rule.
work.example: This goes without saying, but today's content is confidential.

work.title: Product launch
work.description: Presenting a new product's strengths.
work.example: Performance goes without saying, and we were particular about the design too.

etymology: 「言わず」 (negative of 「言う」) + the old wish particle 「もがな」 (“if only …”). Literally “if only it weren't said”, i.e. “better left unsaid”. It later came to mean “needless to say”, close to 「言うまでもない」.

similar.title: 〜は言うまでもなく
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “not to mention A, even B …”. 「言うまでもなく」 is the all-purpose form, fine in speech and writing. 「言わずもがな」 is more elegant and literary, and it also keeps the original sense of “better left unsaid,” which 「言うまでもなく」 lacks.

similar.title: 〜は言うに及ばず
similar.explanation: Close in meaning and also built on 「言う」. 「言うに及ばず」 literally means “there's no need to go as far as saying it.” It is stiffer and more formal, common in official documents and news, and it has only the sense of “needless to say.”

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Also built on 「言う」 and close in meaning. 「言うまでもない」 matches the “goes without saying” use of 「言わずもがなだ」 (「健康が大切なのは言うまでもない」). 「〜までもない」 can follow other verbs too (「説明するまでもない」), whereas 「言わずもがな」 is limited to 「言う」.

similar.title: 〜はおろか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “not to mention A, even B …”. After 「はおろか」 the second part is usually negative, bad, or surprising (「漢字はおろか、ひらがなも書けない」), whereas 「言わずもがな」 is mostly used to add one more positive item.

formation: 「言わず」 is the ない-form of 「言う」 plus the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」, meaning “without saying.” 「もがな」 is an archaic sentence-final particle of wish (built from 「もが」 + 「な」), meaning “if only ….” Put together, it literally means “if only it were left unsaid,” i.e. “better left unsaid.” This is the original sense, which is why 「言わずもがなのことを言う」 means saying something you should have kept quiet about. If it is best left unsaid, it also implies that “everyone understands even without being told,” and that gives the extended meaning “goes without saying.” Then the topic particle 「は」 picks out the obvious item A, and 「も」 adds B after it, forming the pattern “not to mention A, even B …”.

meaning: At the very moment of one action, something else happens unexpectedly.
connection: Verb た-form + 拍子に; noun + の拍子に (何かの拍子に)

senses.label: The moment …
senses.meaning: At the instant of the first action, something unexpected happens as a result. Like “just as …” or “when I …, I accidentally …”. The result is usually accidental and unwelcome.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + 拍子に (転んだ拍子に／立ち上がった拍子に／くしゃみをした拍子に)
examples: As I stood up, I banged my head on the desk.
I hurt my back when I sneezed.
When I fell, my phone screen cracked.

senses.label: Some chance trigger
senses.meaning: 「何かの拍子に」 and 「ふとした拍子に」 mean “for some chance reason”. The speaker doesn't know the exact cause. Often used with 「思い出す」 or 「〜てしまう」.
senses.connection: 何かの拍子に／ふとした拍子に／その拍子に
examples: Sometimes something triggers memories of the past.
By chance, I got to hear what he really thought.

notes: The second part must be an unintended, unexpected event, never a deliberate action: ✕「立ち上がった拍子に、電話をかけた」→ ○「立ち上がった拍子に、コップを倒してしまった」.

The first part is normally a verb in the た-form, meaning “at the moment the action was made”: 「転んだ拍子に」「くしゃみをした拍子に」. It only narrates things that have already happened; it can't be used for the future or for warnings: ✕「立ち上がる拍子に気をつけて」→ ○「立ち上がるときは気をつけて」.

It is most easily confused with 「たとたん」. 「拍子に」 requires that the first action itself (its momentum) triggers the second. When the two merely follow each other in time with no causal link, use 「たとたん」: ✕「家に着いた拍子に雨が降り出した」→ ○「家に着いたとたん、雨が降り出した」.

daily.title: Explaining an injury
daily.description: Telling a friend how you got hurt.
daily.example: I caught my finger when I opened the door.

daily.title: Losing something
daily.description: Telling family how something got lost.
daily.example: I think my keys fell out of my pocket as I got off the train.

daily.title: Talking about memories
daily.description: Chatting with a friend about a sudden memory.
daily.example: Something made me remember my childhood dream.

work.title: Accident report
work.description: Describing what happened in a workplace incident report.
work.example: The worker twisted his ankle as he stepped down from the stepladder.

work.title: News report
work.description: News describing how an accident happened.
work.example: The man is believed to have hit his head hard when he fell.

etymology: 「拍子」 originally means the beat in music or dance. From “a single beat” it came to mean “the instant or momentum of an action”, giving “at the moment of …”.

similar.title: 〜はずみで
similar.explanation: The closest in meaning, and often interchangeable (「転んだはずみで」 / 「転んだ拍子に」). 「はずみ」 (弾み) originally means “rebound, momentum,” so it stresses the force of the impulse, and 「その場のはずみで」 can also mean acting on a momentary impulse. 「拍子に」 focuses on the exact instant of the action.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: Both mean “the moment I did …, …,” and in neither can the second part be the speaker's deliberate act. 「たとたん」 only requires that the two events follow each other closely, with no causal link needed. 「拍子に」 requires the first action to cause the second directly, as in hitting your head as you stood up.

similar.title: 〜や否や／〜や
similar.explanation: Both express events following each other closely in time. 「や否や」 is literary, and its second part can be a deliberate action by the subject (「ベルが鳴るや否や、教室を飛び出した」). With 「拍子に」 the second part can only be an unexpected, involuntary result.

formation: 「拍子」 originally meant the single “beat” in music or dance, and by extension “the instant of an action, the momentum behind it.” 「Vた-form + 拍子」 means “the moment I did …,” and adding the time-point particle 「に」 gives “right at the moment …” Because 「拍子」 itself carries a sense of sudden momentum, the second part is usually an unexpected result swept along by that momentum (bumping your head, breaking something), which is why a deliberate action can't follow. Replace the specific action with something vague such as 「何かの」 or 「ふとした」, and it becomes “owing to some chance trigger.”

meaning: Just as you were about to do something, or had just done it, something unexpected happened.
connection: Verb dictionary form / volitional + とする (た-form) + 矢先に; verb た-form + 矢先に

senses.label: Just as I was about to
senses.meaning: Right when you planned to do something, something else suddenly happened. Like “just as I was about to …”. The result is usually unexpected and bad. Often 「〜ようとした矢先に」 or 「〜と思っていた矢先に」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + 矢先に; 〜ようとした／〜と思っていた + 矢先に
examples: Just as I was about to go out, it started to rain.
Just as I was thinking of contacting him, he called me.
Just as we were leaving home, my child came down with a fever.

senses.label: Right after
senses.meaning: Something went wrong right after you did something. Like “no sooner had I … than …”. Has a regretful “of all times” tone.
senses.connection: Verb た-form + 矢先に／矢先の (〜た矢先の出来事)
examples: No sooner had I bought a house than I was transferred.
I had just quit smoking, and then I smoked again.

notes: The second part is something sudden and beyond control. It can't be a deliberate action by the speaker: ✕「出かけようとした矢先に、傘を持った」→ ○「出かけようとした矢先に、雨が降り出した」.
It only narrates what has already happened; it can't be used for future plans or requests: ✕「出かける矢先に連絡してください」→ ○「出かける前に連絡してください」.

It is most easily confused with 「ところに」. After 「ところに」 the second part can be good or neutral (「困っているところに友達が来てくれた」). 「矢先に」 usually carries regret, “of all moments, right then,” and is mainly used for bad news and accidents.

daily.title: Plans ruined
daily.description: Complaining to a friend that plans fell through right away.
daily.example: Right after I booked the trip, some work came up.

daily.title: Perfect timing
daily.description: Telling someone you were just about to contact them.
daily.example: I was just about to call you!

daily.title: Seen in the news
daily.description: A news story about a tragic accident.
daily.example: The family was speechless at the accident, just before the wedding.

work.title: Reporting to your boss
work.description: Reporting a problem at a key moment in a project.
work.example: Just as we were about to start mass production, we found a defect in a part.

work.title: Business news
work.description: Reporting a company's trouble while expanding.
work.example: Right after it decided to expand overseas, the yen rose sharply.

etymology: 「矢先」 originally means “arrowhead” or the direction an arrow flies. From the moment an arrow is aimed and about to fly, it came to mean “just as something is about to begin”.

similar.title: 〜ところに・〜ところへ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “just as I was in the middle of / about to do something, something else happened.” 「ところに」 is neutral, its second part can be good news (「困っているところに助けが来た」), and it is common in speech. 「矢先に」 is more literary, and its second part is usually an unfortunate surprise.

similar.title: 〜たばかり
similar.explanation: Corresponds to the “just now” sense of 「矢先に」. 「たばかり」 merely states objectively that something has just finished (「家を買ったばかりだ」). 「た矢先に」 is always followed by something that happens right after, with the regret of “of all times, right then.”

similar.title: 〜拍子に
similar.explanation: Both express that something unexpected happened at a certain point in time. With 「拍子に」 the momentum of the action itself directly causes the second part (「立ち上がった拍子に頭をぶつけた」), so there is cause and effect. With 「矢先に」 there is no causal link; the timing is simply bad.

formation: 「矢先」 is 「矢」 (arrow) + 「先」 (tip). It originally meant “arrowhead” and also “the direction an arrow is shot.” The moment an arrow is nocked and aimed at the target is the instant when action is “just about to begin,” which gave the extended meaning “the very moment of starting something.” Adding the time-point 「に」, 「〜ようとした矢先に」 means “just as I was about to …” Being interrupted at that moment naturally brings the tone of “of all times, right then.” After the た-form, it means that things had only just begun (the arrow had barely left the string) when something went wrong.

meaning: You try and try but get nowhere, and you're at a loss and fed up.
connection: Verb ます-stem + あぐねる (考えあぐねる／攻めあぐねる／探しあぐねる)

senses.label: Can't figure it out
senses.meaning: You think it over and over but can't decide. Like “be at a loss over …” or “rack your brains in vain”. Most common: 「考えあぐねる」, 「決めあぐねる」.
senses.connection: 考え／決め／迷い + あぐねる (often with a 「〜か」 question clause)
examples: I've been racking my brains over how to reply.
I couldn't decide on a present, so in the end I just gave money.

senses.label: Trying in vain
senses.meaning: You keep trying but can't reach the goal, and you get tired of it. For example, “can't break through”, “can't find”, “tired of waiting”.
senses.connection: 攻め／探し／待ち + あぐねる
examples: Unable to break through the opponent's solid defense, they went scoreless in the first half.
I couldn't find the shop I was looking for and wandered around the station.
The spring we had waited so long for has finally come.

notes: It only means “kept at it for a long time and still got nowhere, stuck in a deadlock.” It can't be used for simple lack of ability: ✕「一人では持ちあぐねる」→ ○「一人では持てない」.

Don't confuse it with 「かねる」. 「お答えしかねます」 is a polite refusal; 「あぐねる」 only means “can't make up my mind after turning it over and over,” so it can't be used to decline a client: ✕「お答えしあぐねます」→ ○「お答えしかねます」.

It attaches to the ます-stem of only a small set of verbs that involve repeated, continuing effort (「考える」「決める」「攻める」「探す」「待つ」 and so on), and you can't coin new combinations freely. In speech people usually say 「なかなか決められない」.

daily.title: Stuck on a gift
daily.description: Telling a friend you don't know what gift to give.
daily.example: I'm stumped about what to get my mom for her birthday.

daily.title: Seen in sports news
daily.description: Reading a soccer match report.
daily.example: Japan struggled to break through right up to the closing stages.

work.title: Project discussion
work.description: Reporting that a decision hasn't been made.
work.example: We still haven't been able to decide which plan to adopt.

work.title: Social news
work.description: Reporting an issue that drags on unresolved.
work.example: The government is struggling to come up with countermeasures.

etymology: 「あぐねる」 is thought to come from 「あぐむ（倦む）」, “to grow weary”. After a verb, it means you've done something until you're sick of it, with no result.

similar.title: 〜かねる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “hard to do.” 「かねる」 means being unable to do something because of your position or feelings, and it is often used as a polite refusal (「お引き受けしかねます」). 「あぐねる」 means trying repeatedly without result and growing weary of it; it can't be used to refuse.

similar.title: 〜に〜ない (cannot, even if you try)
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「決めるに決められない」 and 「決めあぐねる」 both mean “can't decide, however much I try.” 「〜に〜ない」 stresses being blocked by some cause so that you can't do what you want; 「あぐねる」 stresses the weariness and deadlock that come after repeated thinking or trying.

similar.title: 〜すべがない
similar.explanation: Both can mean “can't think of a way.” 「すべがない」 means there are simply no means at all, nothing to be done (「なすすべがない」); 「考えあぐねる」 means you are still thinking and trying but keep getting nowhere.

formation: 「あぐねる」 is generally thought to come from 「あぐむ」 (倦む), whose original meaning is “to tire of, to get fed up” (the kanji 「倦」 means “weary”). Attached to the ます-stem of a verb as an auxiliary, it works as “do something + get tired of doing it.” People tire of something when they keep doing it with no result, so the whole expression means “can't get anywhere however much I think or try, stuck in a deadlock.” Because it stresses “repetition” and “weariness,” it attaches only to verbs of sustained, repeated effort such as 「考える」「攻める」「探す」「待つ」.

meaning: Manages to carry something difficult through to the end, such as “get away” or “keep it hidden to the end”.
connection: Verb ます-stem + おおせる (逃げおおせる／隠しおおせる／やりおおせる)

senses.label: Pull it off
senses.meaning: Overcome difficulties and fully succeed. Like “manage to …” or “… all the way”. Often used for hard things like escaping or hiding.
senses.connection: 逃げ／隠し／やり + おおせる (often in た-form: 逃げおおせた)
examples: The criminal got away abroad.
I want to praise myself for seeing it through to the end.
He kept the secret hidden right to the end.

senses.label: Can't keep it up
senses.meaning: Often with a negative or rhetorical question: “you can't keep … forever”. For example, 「隠しおおせるものではない」, “it can't stay hidden”. Sounds like a warning or firm statement.
senses.connection: 〜おおせるものではない／〜おおせるはずがない／〜おおせない
examples: You can't hide a lie forever.
Wherever you go, there's no way you'll get away.

notes: It is spelled 「おおせる」 (historical kana 「おほせる」), not 「おうせる」: ✕「逃げおうせる」→ ○「逃げおおせる」.
It attaches only to a small set of verbs for things you can accomplish only by overcoming an obstacle (「逃げる」「隠す」「やる」「言う」 and so on), not to ordinary “finish doing”: ✕「ご飯を食べおおせた」→ ○「ご飯を食べきった」.

「逃げおおせる」 and 「隠しおおせる」 often carry a negative nuance of “someone who shouldn't have gotten away with it.” Saying 「見事に逃げおおせましたね」 to a boss would be taken as sarcasm about dodging responsibility. To praise someone for completing a hard task, use 「やり遂げる」.
The common usage is the negative direction: 「隠しおおせるものではない」 and 「逃げおおせるはずがない」 mean “can't be hidden, can't get away.” Don't read them as “can hide it.”

daily.title: Seen in mystery novels
daily.description: A novel describes how the criminal ends up.
daily.example: The criminal skillfully escaped the police pursuit.

daily.title: Urging a friend to confess
daily.description: A friend wants to hide a mistake; you tell them to be honest.
daily.example: There's no way you can keep that hidden.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on a suspect.
work.example: The suspect had been on the run for over ten years.

work.title: Project wrap-up
work.description: Praising the team for finishing a tough job.
work.example: Despite the tight schedule, we all saw it through to the end.

etymology: 「おおせる」 is written 「果せる」 or 「遂せる」 and originally meant “to complete, achieve”. In modern Japanese it is almost never used alone, only as an auxiliary after another verb.

similar.title: 〜きる・〜きれない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “seeing it through to the end.” 「きる」 just means “completely finishing” and attaches to many verbs (「食べきる」「使いきる」). 「おおせる」 stresses finally getting away with it despite difficulty or interference, and attaches to only a few verbs. 「逃げきる」 usually means keeping the lead to the finish line in a race, while 「逃げおおせる」 usually means escaping capture.

similar.title: 〜抜く
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express holding out to the end. 「抜く」 stresses the hardship and thoroughness of the process (「走り抜く」「考え抜く」) and is mostly positive. 「おおせる」 stresses the final result, “I did it and wasn't found out,” and is often used in negative contexts such as escape or concealment.

similar.title: 〜通す
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: 「隠し通す」 and 「隠しおおせる」 can both mean “keep it hidden to the end.” 「通す」 stresses the will to carry the same action through from start to finish; 「おおせる」 stresses ultimate success without being exposed.

similar.title: 〜てのける
similar.explanation: Both express accomplishing a difficult task. 「てのける」 stresses doing it neatly and nonchalantly, and carries admiration or surprise. 「おおせる」 stresses overcoming obstacles and succeeding only by holding out to the end.

formation: 「おおせる」 is written 「果せる」 or 「遂せる」, and is generally thought to mean originally “to complete, to carry through,” related to 「果たす」 and 「遂げる」. In modern Japanese it is almost never used alone, only as an auxiliary after the ます-stem of a verb: 「逃げ + おおせる」 = “carry out the escape to the end” = “succeed in getting away.” Carrying something through presupposes obstacles along the way (pursuit, exposure), so it attaches to verbs like running away or hiding, where success means never being found out. That is also why it pairs with 「ものではない」 and 「はずがない」, meaning “you can't keep that up to the end.”

meaning: Pulls off something difficult neatly, or calmly does or says something most people wouldn't dare.
connection: Verb te-form + のける (やってのける／言ってのける)

senses.label: Pull it off brilliantly
senses.meaning: Easily and skillfully achieves something most people find hard. Carries admiration. Most common: 「やってのける」.
senses.connection: やって + のける (often with 「見事に」, 「あっさり」, 「簡単に」)
examples: He brilliantly pulled off that difficult surgery.
Though he's a newcomer, he landed a big contract with ease.

senses.label: Do it without batting an eye
senses.meaning: Says or does something shocking that others wouldn't dare, as if it were nothing. Can be admiring or critical. Often with 「平然と」, 「平気で」, 「堂々と」.
senses.connection: 言って／して + のける (平然と〜てのける)
examples: She boldly voiced her objection right in front of the president.
He badmouths people without batting an eye.

notes: Only for things done on purpose and successfully, never for mistakes: ✕「財布を落としてのけた」→ ○「財布を落としてしまった」.
「言ってのける」 and 「平気でやってのける」 often carry criticism of someone nonchalant and lacking restraint. Saying 「よく言ってのけましたね」 to a boss sounds sarcastic; to express admiration, say 「さすがですね」.
Using it about yourself (「私が見事にやってのけました」) sounds boastful. When reporting to a superior, 「無事にやり遂げることができました」 is more appropriate.
The kanji 「退ける」 on its own is normally read 「しりぞける」 (to repel, to reject). This grammar point is usually written in kana as 「のける」, so be careful not to confuse them when reading.

daily.title: Praising a friend
daily.description: A friend did something hard alone, and you're impressed.
daily.example: You handled the whole move by yourself? That's amazing.

daily.title: Complaining about someone
daily.description: Talking with a friend about someone who's very blunt.
daily.example: That person says terrible things without batting an eye, right?

work.title: Praising a subordinate
work.description: A manager praises a team member at a meeting.
work.example: Pulling off this project in such a short time was superb.

work.title: Sports news
work.description: Reporting an athlete's difficult move.
work.example: On the big stage, he landed a quadruple jump twice.

etymology: 「のける」 is written 「退ける」 and originally means “move aside, remove”. As an auxiliary it means “dispose of a task cleanly”, which led to “pull off neatly” and “do without a second thought”.

similar.title: 〜てみせる
similar.explanation: Both relate to the ability to “do it and show them.” 「てみせる」 usually states the speaker's resolve about the future (「絶対合格してみせる」, “I'll pass, just watch”). 「てのける」 is mostly used to describe something already accomplished, with an onlooker's admiration or surprise.

similar.title: 〜おおせる
similar.explanation: Both express accomplishing a difficult task. 「おおせる」 stresses clearing obstacles and succeeding only by holding on to the end (「逃げおおせる」). 「てのける」 stresses doing it neatly and effortlessly.

similar.title: 〜てしまう
similar.explanation: Both attach to the て-form and express completion of an action, so they are often compared. 「てしまう」 can express regret or irreversibility, and can be used for mistakes. 「てのける」 is used only for things done on purpose, stresses decisiveness and neatness, and carries no sense of regret.

formation: 「のける」 is written 「退ける」 and originally means “to move something aside, to get it out of the way” (as in 「押しのける」). Attached to the て-form as an auxiliary, it works as “do something + dispose of it in one go.” Pushing an obstacle aside cleanly implies a decisive, neat action, which produced the meaning “to pull off a difficult task with flair.” At the same time, “moving aside” can also mean brushing other people's concerns and rules out of the way, which extended it to “do or say, as if it were nothing, what others wouldn't dare.” That is why 「言ってのける」 can be either praise or criticism.

meaning: There's no room at all for something; it doesn't matter. Scornful and impatient. Crude spoken Japanese.
connection: Noun + もへったくれもない／もへったくれもあるか

senses.label: Forget about …
senses.meaning: In this situation, the thing mentioned simply doesn't count. Like “… my foot” or “to hell with …”. Rude and scornful.
senses.connection: Noun (規則・常識・マナー・作戦 etc.) + もへったくれもない
examples: In an emergency like this, forget the rules.
All that matters is winning. Strategy, schmategy.

senses.label: Who cares about …?
senses.meaning: The rhetorical 「〜もへったくれもあるか」 strongly denies it: “who has time for …?” Even harsher than 「ない」.
senses.connection: Noun + もへったくれもあるか／あるもんか
examples: When you're starving, who cares about manners?
At this point, why hold back?

notes: It is very vulgar. Used with superiors, clients, elders, or in formal settings, it sounds uncouth and rude. For the same meaning in formal settings, use 「〜などと言っている場合ではない」.
Using it to dismiss something the other person values (「お前の理屈もへったくれもない」) is treating it with contempt, and in an argument it easily escalates. Be especially careful.

It looks like 「〜もなんともない」 and is easily confused with it. 「痛くもなんともない」 means “doesn't hurt at all” (denying a feeling), while 「〜もへったくれもない」 attaches only to nouns and contemptuously denies the value of something: ✕「痛くもへったくれもない」.

daily.title: Griping to friends
daily.description: Annoyed at being asked to follow rules in an emergency.
daily.example: It's a fire! Forget about waiting your turn!

daily.title: Seen in manga
daily.description: A line from a rough-mannered manga character.
daily.example: To hell with logic, we just do it!

daily.title: Within the family
daily.description: A father tells a family member not to be so polite.
daily.example: We're family. No need to hold back.

work.title: Quoted in a commentary
work.description: A column quotes someone's crude words to describe chaos.
work.example: Reportedly, the site was in a state of “manuals be damned”.

etymology: 「へったくれ」 is slang for belittling something, like “worthless thing”. Its origin is unclear; one theory links it to 「屁（へ）」 (fart).

similar.title: 〜どころではない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning: “no time for rules in an emergency” can also be 「規則どころではない」. 「どころではない」 is a neutral “no room to think about it” and can be used in formal settings. 「もへったくれもない」 is contemptuous and rude, and is only for casual talk among people who know each other well.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: Both express disregard for something one ought to take into account. 「もかまわず」 objectively describes doing something regardless of …, in a neutral tone (「人目もかまわず泣いた」). 「もへったくれもない」 is the speaker's contemptuous denial of the thing's value.

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (disparaging)
similar.explanation: Both can express contempt for something. 「なんか」 is milder and widely used (「規則なんか関係ない」). 「もへったくれもない」 is more contemptuous and more vulgar, and appears only in the fixed forms 「〜もへったくれもない」 and 「〜もへったくれもあるか」.

formation: 「へったくれ」 is a slang word for belittling things, roughly “worthless junk, something not worth mentioning,” of unknown origin (one theory links it to 「屁」). The pattern 「Aもへったくれもない」 is built like 「Aも何もない」: with 「も〜も」 it lists A alongside “worthless junk” and negates them together. Putting A next to “something not worth mentioning” itself belittles A, so the whole means “what do you mean, A? It's out of the question, no time for that.” Turning it into the rhetorical question 「〜もへったくれもあるか」, “where is there any A?”, makes the denial even stronger.

meaning: The very best in a group or era; second to none.
connection: Noun (organization / area / era) + きっての + noun

senses.label: Best in the group
senses.meaning: The most outstanding in a group or area. Like “the best … in …”. Usually followed by a noun for a person or evaluation, like 「秀才」, 「名門」, 「実力者」.
senses.connection: クラス／社内／町／業界 + きっての + noun
examples: He's the brightest student in the class.
This shop is known as the oldest, most established in town.
She's the biggest idea person in the company.

senses.label: Best of the era
senses.meaning: After a word for an era or period: “the most … of this time”. Common in 「当代きっての」 and 「近年きっての」. Formal.
senses.connection: 当代／近年／戦後 + きっての + noun
examples: He is said to be the finest actor of his day.
The biggest typhoon in recent years made landfall.

notes: It is used only for positive evaluation or objective descriptions like “the largest.” Used for a negative person it sounds awkward: ✕「クラスきっての怠け者」→ ○「クラス一の怠け者」.
What precedes it must be a noun that sets a range (an organization, region, or era), and a noun must follow: ✕「彼はクラスきってだ」→ ○「彼はクラスきっての秀才だ」.
The evaluation is strong, so using it to introduce yourself (「私は社内きっての営業マンです」) sounds like boasting. In a self-introduction, a plain phrase like 「営業を担当しております」 is better.

daily.title: Introducing a friend
daily.description: Introducing a well-known friend to someone.
daily.example: He was the best soccer player at our university, you know.

daily.title: Seen in travel guides
daily.description: A brochure introducing famous local shops.
daily.example: This is the most popular ramen shop in the prefecture.

work.title: Personnel announcement
work.description: Introducing a newly transferred manager.
work.example: Our new department head is the industry's top sales expert.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting on a famous person.
work.example: The leading writer of our time has released a new work.

etymology: 「きって」 is thought to come from the te-form of 「切る」, meaning “picked out from among …”. Hence “the most outstanding in a range”.

similar.title: 〜の中で〜がいちばん
similar.explanation: Same meaning; both express “the most … among …”. 「の中で〜がいちばん」 is the everyday form and combines freely with adjectives (「クラスの中で彼がいちばん背が高い」). 「きっての」 is literary and formal, only modifies a noun, and carries high praise.

similar.title: 〜をおいて
similar.explanation: Both express very high evaluation. 「AをおいてBはいない」 means “there is no one but A,” stressing the only suitable person (「この仕事を任せられるのは彼をおいてほかにいない」). 「きっての」 only says “the best within the range of A” and doesn't stress uniqueness.

similar.title: 〜にかけては
similar.explanation: Both can say that someone is “number one.” 「にかけては」 limits the field (「料理にかけては誰にも負けない」, “nobody beats me when it comes to cooking”). 「きっての」 limits a group, region, or era.

formation: 「きって」 is generally thought to come from the て-form 「切って」 of the verb 「切る」, used here in the sense of “to single out from the whole.” 「Aきっての」 literally means “singled out from the range A,” and 「の」 links it to the noun that follows. What gets singled out of the whole range is naturally the most outstanding one, hence “the best in A.” Because it means “choosing within a range,” a range noun must come before it and the person or thing being evaluated must follow.

meaning: Once you start, there's no end to it. Often about listing things, fussing or worrying.
connection: Verb ば-form + きりがない (also 〜たら／〜と きりがない)

senses.label: Endless list
senses.meaning: If you start listing or naming things, you'll never finish. Like “there's no end to …”. Often with 「言う」, 「挙げる」, 「数える」. It implies “so let's leave it there”.
senses.connection: 言えば／挙げれば／数えれば + きりがない
examples: If I start complaining, there's no end to it.
If you list his faults, you'll never finish.
You could always want more, but overall I'm satisfied.

senses.label: Endless worry
senses.meaning: Worrying, fussing or comparing never ends. Used to tell yourself or others to stop. Often with 「心配する」, 「気にする」, 「上を見る」.
senses.connection: 心配すれば／気にし出したら／上を見ると + きりがない
examples: Worrying will never end, so let's go to bed.
Once you start fussing over details, there's no end.
There's always someone better off.

notes: The first part is an act the speaker actively takes, such as saying, listing, comparing, or worrying, and the meaning is “once you start, there's no end.” It does not describe objective quantity: ✕「この町には店がきりがない」→ ○「この町には数えきれないほど店がある」.
It carries the implication “so let's leave it there.” Answering a superior's or client's complaint with 「言えばきりがないですよ」 tells them to stop, which sounds impatient and rude.
Don't mix it up with 「限りがない」. 「宇宙には限りがない」 is an objective “endless” and has none of the subjective tone of “if I started, there'd be no end, so forget it.”

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend has many complaints about a new place; you say be content.
daily.example: Complaining never ends. Being close to the station is good enough, isn't it?

daily.title: Hesitating while shopping
daily.description: Choosing something with family and comparing endlessly.
daily.example: Comparing will go on forever, so let's go with this one.

daily.title: Parenting worries
daily.description: Mothers chatting about their kids.
daily.example: When it comes to kids, there's no end to worrying, is there?

work.title: Wrapping up a meeting
work.description: The chair ends the discussion and moves to decisions.
work.example: We could list improvements forever, so let's set priorities.

work.title: Project management
work.description: Reminding the team not to chase perfection forever.
work.example: Perfection has no end. Let's get it into a form we can ship on time.

etymology: 「きり」 is written 「切り」, meaning “break, end point, limit”. 「きりがない」 means “there's no end”. After a conditional, it means “once you start, there's no end”.

similar.title: 〜きる・〜きれない
similar.explanation: Same origin; both come from 「切る」. 「数えきれない」 and 「言いきれない」 mean objectively “can't finish counting/saying them all.” 「数えればきりがない」 means subjectively “once you start counting, there's no end,” often with the implication “so I won't.”

similar.title: 〜きり
similar.explanation: Same origin: 「きり」 comes from 「切り」, the noun form of 「切る」, meaning “limit, endpoint.” 「〜きり」 means “only …” or “nothing since …” (「行ったきり帰らない」). 「きりがない」 means “no endpoint, endless.”

similar.title: 〜てもしょうがない・〜ても仕方がない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning, and often interchangeable when urging someone to stop worrying (「心配してもしょうがない」 / 「心配すればきりがない」). 「てもしょうがない」 looks at “it's no use doing it”; 「ばきりがない」 looks at “once you start doing it, it never ends.”

formation: 「きり」 is written 「切り」, the noun form of the verb 「切る」, meaning “a cutting point, a break, an end” (as in 「区切り」 and 「切りのいいところ」). 「きりがない」 = “there is no place to cut” = “endless.” Adding the conditional 「〜ば」 (or 「〜たら」, 「〜と」) in front gives “once you start …, there is no break at which to stop.” Because it stresses that there is no stopping point, it is often used to tell yourself or others to just stop here, and so it is often followed by 「から」 or 「が」, leading into “forget it” or “but …”.

meaning: Even if it fails, you're just back where you started, with nothing lost. So it's worth a try.
connection: Verb te-form + もともとだ; だめでもともと (short: 「だめもと」)

senses.label: Nothing to lose
senses.meaning: You never expected success, so failing costs nothing. Like “it's fine if …, I had nothing to begin with”. Used to encourage yourself or others to try boldly.
senses.connection: 断られて／負けて／だめで + もともと（だ）
examples: We have nothing to lose, so let's ask the president directly.
Thinking I had nothing to lose if she said no, I asked her out.
We've got nothing to lose by losing, so let's go all out.

senses.label: Casual short form
senses.meaning: In speech, 「だめでもともと」 is shortened to 「だめもと」 and used as a noun. 「だめもとで〜」 means “just giving it a shot”.
senses.connection: だめもと + で〜てみる／だめもとだけど
examples: I applied just to give it a shot, and amazingly I got in.
I asked for a discount, just on the off chance.

notes: The first part can only be a bad result such as failure, rejection, or losing. A good result makes no sense: ✕「合格してもともとだ」→ ○「落ちてもともとだ」.
Asking someone with 「だめもとでお願いします」 tells them “I wasn't counting on you saying yes,” which is rude to a superior or client. Say 「無理を承知でお願いいたします」 instead.
Don't confuse it with the adverb 「もともと」 (“originally”). 「彼はもともと静かな人だ」 is not this grammar point; here, 「〜て」 or 「〜で」 always comes before it.

daily.title: Encouraging a confession
daily.description: A friend is afraid to confess their feelings; you encourage them.
daily.example: You've got nothing to lose even if she turns you down, so tell her how you feel.

daily.title: Entering a lottery
daily.description: Talking with a friend about a prize draw.
daily.example: Nothing to lose if I don't win, so I'll enter.

daily.title: Asking anyway
daily.description: What you want is sold out, but you'll ask at the shop anyway.
daily.example: Let's ask the staff if they have any in stock, just in case.

work.title: Going after a client
work.description: Proposing to your boss to approach a tough client.
work.example: We have nothing to lose, so please let me pitch them once.

work.title: Negotiating terms
work.description: Discussing a negotiation with a coworker.
work.example: Nothing to lose if they refuse, so let's ask for a deadline extension.

etymology: 「もともと（元々）」 means “originally”. 「〜てもともと」 literally means “even if …, you're just back to how things were”, i.e. nothing lost.

similar.title: 〜てもかまわない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can express “even if …, it doesn't matter” (「断られてもかまわない」). 「てもかまわない」 only expresses concession and permission. 「てもともと」 goes further and gives a reason: you weren't counting on it anyway, so failing costs nothing, which encourages you to try boldly.

similar.title: 〜たところで
similar.explanation: Both first suppose a less-than-ideal result and then say “no big deal.” 「たところで」 usually leads to a pessimistic conclusion, “even if you do it, it's useless” (「今さら謝ったところで許してもらえない」), and discourages action. 「てもともと」 means “you lose nothing by failing” and encourages action.

formation: 「もともと」 (元々) means “the original state.” 「Negative result in て-form (で after nouns and な-adjectives) + 元々 (だ)」 literally means “even if it ends up as …, you're only back where you started.” If the worst outcome (failure, rejection) merely leaves you where you began, nothing is lost. If nothing is lost, there is no reason not to try, so the whole brings a positive tone of “you may as well give it a shot.” In speech 「だめで元々」 is shortened to 「だめもと」 and used as a noun (「だめもとで頼む」).

meaning: A rhetorical “as if I'd …!” / “I won't let …!”, showing strong determination or resistance. Spoken.
connection: Verb te-form + たまるか (たまるものか／たまるもんか)

senses.label: No way I'll … (resolve)
senses.meaning: The speaker is determined never to do something. Like “there's no way I'll …”. Common: 「負けてたまるか」, 「あきらめてたまるか」. Very intense, often used to psych yourself up.
senses.connection: 負けて／あきらめて／やめて + たまるか
examples: There's no way I'm losing here!
After coming this far, there's no way I'll give up.

senses.label: I won't let it happen
senses.meaning: Strong resistance to something unfair; you won't allow it. Often follows a passive or an unwanted state. Like “I won't let …” or “as if I'd let …”.
senses.connection: Passive verb te-form／〜なって + たまるか
examples: I won't let a guy like that make a fool of me!
I'm not dying over something like this!
Just swallow it and let it go? No way!

notes: It looks like 「〜てたまらない」 but means something entirely different: 「負けてたまるか」 is “I won't lose,” while 「悔しくてたまらない」 is “I'm unbearably frustrated.” Drop the 「か」 or switch to 「ない」 and the resolve turns into “… beyond endurance.”

The verb before it is something the speaker does not want to happen, not something they want to do: ✕「勝ってたまるか」 (meaning “I'll win no matter what”) → ○「負けてたまるか」. Reversing it gives the opposite meaning.
The tone is fierce and rough. Saying 「そんな条件、のんでたまるか」 to a superior or client will be taken as defiance. In formal situations, decline with 「お受けいたしかねます」.

daily.title: Psyching yourself up
daily.description: An athlete who is behind encourages themself.
daily.example: It's not over yet. I'm not going to lose!

daily.title: After being mocked
daily.description: Laughed at by a friend, you decide to prove them wrong.
daily.example: I won't let him keep laughing at me. I'll show him for sure.

daily.title: Seen in novels
daily.description: A hero's inner voice in a crisis.
daily.example: “I can't let it end here,” he thought, gritting his teeth.

work.title: Rallying the team
work.description: After a setback, the project lead speaks to the team.
work.example: We've prepared this long. We're not letting a competitor take it!

etymology: 「たまる」 is written 「堪る」, meaning “to bear, to endure”. 「〜てたまるか」 is literally “if …, could I bear it?”, a rhetorical “absolutely not”, which turned into a resolve: “never!”.

similar.title: 〜てたまらない
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built on 「堪る」. 「てたまらない」 uses the negative to mean “unbearably …” and describes strong feeling (「嬉しくてたまらない」). 「てたまるか」 uses a rhetorical question to mean “I won't allow …” and expresses resolve or resistance.

similar.title: 〜ものか・〜もんか
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both use a rhetorical question to mean “never …”. 「ものか」 often follows the speaker's own volitional action (「二度と行くものか」, “I'll never go there again”). Before 「てたまるか」 comes mostly something unwanted (「負ける」「馬鹿にされる」), expressing resistance to letting it happen, in a fiercer tone.

similar.title: 〜まい
similar.explanation: Both can express negative resolve. 「まい」 is literary and calm (「二度と言うまい」). 「てたまるか」 is colloquial and emotional, with anger or fighting spirit.

formation: 「たまる」 is written 「堪る」, meaning “to endure, to withstand,” and in modern Japanese it mostly appears in the negative 「たまらない」. 「〜て + たまる + か」 literally means “having done …, can I bear it?”, and the rhetorical 「か」 means “I absolutely cannot bear it.” Being unable to bear something happening means being determined not to let it happen, which gives “never …” and “how could I …!” With 「〜てたまるものか／もんか」 the exclamatory 「もの」 is added and the tone gets stronger.

meaning: A strong denial: “not … at all”, “nothing of the sort”.
connection: Noun / な-adjective stem + でもなんでもない

senses.label: Not … at all
senses.meaning: After a noun, flatly denies an identity or quality. Like “no … at all” or “far from …”. Much stronger than 「〜ではない」, often with irritation or self-defense.
senses.connection: Noun + でもなんでもない (友達／専門家／天才 etc.)
examples: He's no friend of mine. Just an acquaintance.
This is not art at all.
I'm by no means an expert.

senses.label: Not the least bit
senses.meaning: After a な-adjective, means you have none of that quality or feeling. Like “not the least bit …”. Often used to rebut someone's guess.
senses.connection: な-adjective stem + でもなんでもない (好き／特別／簡単 etc.)
examples: I don't like him one bit.
This problem isn't hard at all.

notes: It attaches only to nouns and な-adjectives. For い-adjectives, say 「〜くもなんともない」: ✕「痛いでもなんでもない」→ ○「痛くもなんともない」.
It is easy to reverse with 「〜わけではない」. 「好きなわけではない」 is the softer “it's not that I like it,” while 「好きでもなんでもない」 means “I don't like it one bit.” Misusing it turns a gentle remark into a flat refusal.
The denial is thorough. Aimed directly at the other person or something they treasure (「あなたの作品は芸術でもなんでもない」), it can hurt badly. When judging someone's work, say something like 「〜とは言いにくい」.

daily.title: Denying a relationship
daily.description: A friend thinks you're dating someone; you quickly deny it.
daily.example: No, he's not my boyfriend or anything!

daily.title: Rejecting “help”
daily.description: Someone says it's for your own good; you disagree.
daily.example: That's not kindness at all. It's just meddling.

work.title: Humbly clarifying
work.description: Asked for advice as if you were an expert, you explain your position.
work.example: I'm by no means a legal expert, so please check the details with a lawyer.

work.title: Opinion piece
work.description: A commentator says a policy isn't what it claims.
work.example: This is no reform at all. It's just a price hike.

etymology: 「でも」 (“even, say”) + 「なんでも」 (“anything”) + 「ない」. Literally “it's not …, nor anything else”, which gives a total denial.

similar.title: 〜もなんともない
similar.explanation: Same structure and close in meaning; both are thorough denials, “neither A nor anything else.” 「でもなんでもない」 attaches to nouns and な-adjectives and mostly denies identity or nature. 「〜くもなんともない」 attaches to い-adjectives and so on and mostly denies a feeling (「痛くもなんともない」).

similar.title: 〜なんか・〜など (disparaging)
similar.explanation: Both can deny an identity or thing. 「〜なんかじゃない」 has a tone of disdain, coyness, or modesty (「友達なんかじゃない」). 「でもなんでもない」 emphasizes a calm, thorough denial of identity or nature.

similar.title: 〜わけではない
similar.explanation: Both are negations, but the strength differs greatly: 「好きなわけではない」 is a softer partial denial, “it's not that I like it,” while 「好きでもなんでもない」 is a total denial, “I don't like it at all.”

formation: It is made of 「でも」 + 「なんでも」 (何でも) + 「ない」. 「Aでも」 is “is A,” and 「なんでも」 is “(is) anything else”; the two are listed together and both negated by 「ない」, so it literally means “it is neither A nor anything else.” Negating even “anything else” wipes out A completely, far stronger than 「Aではない」 alone. The 「で」 in the structure is the continuative form of the copula 「だ」, so a noun or the stem of a な-adjective precedes it; い-adjectives don't take 「で」 and use 「〜くもなんともない」 instead.

meaning: Classical expression for “about to …” or “trying to …”, like 「〜ようとする」. Written and literary.
connection: Verb ない-stem + んとする (する→せんとする)

senses.label: About to …
senses.meaning: A state or change is just about to happen. Like “about to …” or “on the verge of …”. Often with 「今まさに」; mostly for describing scenes.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + んとする／んとしている (沈まんとする／終わらんとする)
examples: The sun is just now about to set.
The long winter is finally coming to an end.
Just as the train was about to depart, a man jumped aboard.

senses.label: Trying to …
senses.meaning: The subject intends to do something. Like “seek to …” or “attempt to …”. Solemn; common in speeches, editorials and declarations.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + んとする (明らかにせんとする／切り開かんとする)
examples: He risked his life seeking to bring the truth to light.
I want to support the young people who are trying to open up a new era.

notes: It attaches to the ない-form (mizenkei) of a verb, not the dictionary form: ✕「沈むんとする」→ ○「沈まんとする」. 「する」 becomes 「せんとする」; 「しんとする」 means “quiet, silent” and is not this grammar point.
This 「ん」 is the archaic 「む」 of volition and conjecture, not a negative. Don't read it like the Kansai dialect 「行かん」 (“won't go”): 「行かんとする」 means “about to go,” not “not going.”
It is an archaic, literary expression. Saying 「今から帰らんとしております」 to a boss sounds affectedly stiff, even comical. In everyday speech, use 「〜ようとする」.

daily.title: Seen in novels
daily.description: A tense scene in a novel.
daily.example: Just as the door was about to open, the lights went out.

daily.title: Documentary subtitles
daily.description: Narration describing a natural landscape.
daily.example: Climbers gathered on the summit as the morning sun was about to rise.

work.title: Formal speech
work.description: A solemn address at a ceremony.
work.example: Our company is now about to take a new step forward.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial on the government's intentions.
work.example: The government appears to be trying to dodge public criticism.

etymology: 「ん」 is a sound change of the classical auxiliary 「む」, which shows will or conjecture. 「とする」 means “intend, be about to”. Together: “about to …” or “trying to …”. The modern equivalent is 「〜ようとする」.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うとする
similar.explanation: Same meaning and same origin (「(よ)う」 is also generally thought to come from archaic 「む」). 「ようとする」 is the standard modern form, fine in speech and writing. 「んとする」 is a survival of classical Japanese, used only in writing, speeches, and literary description, with a solemn tone.

similar.title: 〜んばかりに／〜んばかりの
similar.explanation: Same origin; the 「ん」 is archaic 「む」 in both. 「んばかり」 means “almost, as if about to …”; it hasn't actually happened, and it is mostly a hyperbolic figure of speech (「泣かんばかりに頼んだ」). 「んとする」 means it is truly about to happen or that someone really intends to do it.

similar.title: 〜んがため（に）
similar.explanation: Same origin; 「んがため」 is 「む」 + 「が」 + 「ため」, expressing the strong purpose “in order to …” (「勝たんがために手段を選ばない」). 「んとする」 expresses intention or imminence and does not express purpose by itself.

formation: 「ん」 is a sound change of the classical auxiliary 「む」, expressing volition (“will …”) or conjecture (“will …”), and attaches to the mizenkei (ない-form) of a verb: 「沈ま + む」 → 「沈まん」. 「と」 is a quotation particle, and 「する」 means “intend to / be in the state of.” Together, 「沈まんとする」 means “be in the state of ‘about to sink’”: with a will-bearing subject it is “try to …,” and without will it is “be about to …” This corresponds exactly to modern 「〜(よ)うとする」, whose 「(よ)う」 is generally thought to have developed from 「む」 as well.

connection: Verb ない-stem + ずして (する→せずして)

senses.label: Without doing …
senses.meaning: The result happens without the first action ever taking place. Like “without …ing”. Common in 「戦わずして勝つ」 and 「労せずして」.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずして + result (戦わずして／労せずして)
examples: Winning without fighting is the best strategy.
He got a fortune without lifting a finger.

senses.label: Without …, no …
senses.meaning: With a negative or rhetorical question after it: “without doing A, B is impossible”. Close to 「〜なくしては」.
senses.connection: Verb ない-stem + ずして + 〜ない／〜ありえない／〜だろうか
examples: There is no success without effort.
You can't make the right call without seeing the site.

senses.label: Before … / unexpectedly
senses.meaning: In set phrases: “before … even …” or “without intending”. For example, 「一年を待たずして」 “in less than a year”, 「期せずして」 “by chance, without planning”.
senses.connection: 〜を待たずして／期せずして／時を経ずして
examples: He quit the company in less than a year.
Without planning it, the two came up with the same answer.

notes: 「する」 becomes 「せずして」: ✕「努力しずして」→ ○「努力せずして」.

The “can't … without …” meaning has to be echoed by a negative or rhetorical question in the second part; without the negation the meaning changes. 「努力せずして成功した」 is “succeeded without effort,” while 「努力せずして成功はない」 is “there is no success without effort.”
The tone is stiff and archaic. In everyday conversation or emails to colleagues, use 「〜ないで」 or 「〜ずに」; overusing it sounds pretentious.

daily.title: Seen in historical novels
daily.description: A novel describes a famous general's strategy.
daily.example: He took the castle without losing a single soldier.

daily.title: Seen in sayings
daily.description: Reading an inspirational quote.
daily.example: What is gained without effort is soon lost.

work.title: Business commentary
work.description: An article stresses the importance of practice.
work.example: Without listening to customers, no good products are born.

work.title: News report
work.description: Reporting an official's quick resignation.
work.example: The new minister resigned less than a month after taking office.

etymology: The classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 + the connective 「して」, equal to modern 「〜ないで」. Common in readings of classical Chinese texts, as in 「戦わずして人の兵を屈す」.

similar.title: 〜なくして（は）
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can express “without …, can't …”. 「なくして」 attaches to nouns (「努力なくして成功はない」); 「ずして」 attaches to verbs (「努力せずして」) and can also mean “without doing …, (achieved it),” which 「なくして」 can't.

similar.title: 〜ことなしに
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “without doing …, (can/can't) …”. 「ことなしに」 attaches to the dictionary form and is modern written language; 「ずして」 attaches to the ない-stem, is more archaic, and appears mostly in set phrases and maxims.

similar.title: 〜ずに
similar.explanation: Same origin and close in meaning; both contain the negative auxiliary 「ず」 and express “… without …”. 「ずに」 is the ordinary modern form. 「ずして」 is archaic and stiff, and often pairs with a negative second part to mean “can't … without …”.

similar.title: 〜ずとも
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are built on 「ず」. 「ずとも」 expresses concession, “even without …, …” (「言わずとも分かる」). 「ずして」 expresses manner or condition, “… without …” / “can't … without …”.

formation: 「ず」 is the classical negative auxiliary, attached to the mizenkei (ない-form) of a verb to mean “not …”; 「して」 is a classical conjunctive particle equivalent to modern 「て」. So 「〜ずして」 means “without …, and …,” structurally the classical version of 「〜ないで」 and 「〜ずに」. How the two clauses relate depends on the second part: if it is an achieved result, it means “did … without doing …” (「戦わずして勝つ」); if it is negative or a rhetorical question, it means “can't … without doing …” (「努力せずして成功はない」). 「待たずして」 and 「期せずして」 are set phrases that grew out of this structure.

meaning: Something happened as a matter of course, inevitably. Can also mean “it can be done in theory, but it's hard in practice”. Written.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べくして + same verb in た-form (起こるべくして起こった)

senses.label: Was bound to
senses.meaning: The same verb appears twice: “what was bound to happen happened”. Like “was bound to …” or “was destined to …”. Mostly used when analyzing causes afterward.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べくして + same verb た-form (する→すべくして)
examples: This accident, you could say, was bound to happen.
They won because they deserved to win.
Maybe the two were destined to meet.

senses.label: Easier said than done
senses.meaning: With a negative or “hard” after it: “you can do it in theory, but in practice it's hard”. Classical in tone; mostly in sayings.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べくして + 〜難し／〜難い／〜ない
examples: Easier said than done.
Ideals are easy to talk about, but not easy to realize.

notes: For the “inevitable” meaning, the same verb is used before and after, with the past tense in the second part: ✕「起こるべくして事故になった」→ ○「起こるべくして起こった」.

Don't confuse it with 「〜べく」 (“in order to”). 「勝つべく努力した」 is “worked hard in order to win,” while 「勝つべくして勝った」 is “won, as was only to be expected.” Without 「して」 the meaning shifts from “inevitability” to “purpose.”

「負けるべくして負けた」 and 「失敗するべくして失敗した」 are harsh verdicts meaning “was bound to lose, deserved to lose.” Said in front of the person concerned they sting badly, so be careful when commenting on someone else's failure.

daily.example: With that little preparation, they were bound to lose.

etymology: The continuative form 「べく」 of the classical auxiliary 「べし」 + the connective 「して」. 「べし」 means “naturally, should”, so 「〜べくして〜」 means “as it naturally should”, i.e. inevitably.

similar.title: 〜べく
similar.explanation: Same origin; both are the continuative form 「べく」 of 「べし」. 「べく」 alone after a verb expresses purpose, “in order to …” (「合格すべく努力した」). 「べくして」 repeats the same verb before and after to mean “inevitably …” and has no purpose meaning.

similar.title: 〜べくもない
similar.explanation: Same origin; both contain 「べく」. 「べくもない」 means “there is no way to …” (「知るべくもない」), denying possibility. 「べくして」 means “it happened as it was bound to,” affirming inevitability.

similar.title: 〜べし
similar.explanation: Same origin; the 「べく」 in 「べくして」 is the continuative form of 「べし」. 「べし」 itself means “should, must” (「学生は勉強すべし」) and appears mostly in slogans and rules. 「べくして」 is used only for after-the-fact judgments that “it was bound to be so.”

similar.title: 〜て当然だ
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both express “only natural.” 「て当然だ」 is the common modern form and can be used for things that haven't happened (「怒って当然だ」). 「べくして〜た」 is literary, used only for things that have happened, and repeats the same verb before and after.

formation: 「べく」 is the continuative form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」, which means “should, as is only proper.” 「して」 is a classical conjunctive particle equivalent to 「て」. 「V-べくして V-た」 literally means “did V as it was proper to V,” i.e. “it should happen by reason, and indeed it happened,” hence “inevitably, destined.” Repeating the same verb sets “what should be” beside “what actually was” and stresses that the two match exactly. If the second part is not the same verb but “difficult” or “can't,” it becomes the other pattern, “should be able to, but in practice is hard” (「言うべくして行うは難し」).
